title: Cache Performance Analysis: AMAT and the Memory Hierarchy

sections.heading: Hit time, miss rate, miss penalty
sections.body:
Three numbers describe a cache, and the whole of cache performance analysis is the algebra that combines them.

- **Miss rate** $m$ is misses divided by references; the hit rate is $1-m$. CENG331 quotes 3–10% for a typical L1 and often well under 1% for L2.
- **Hit time** $T_h$ is the time to deliver a line that *is* in the cache — including set selection, tag comparison and word selection, not just the data transfer. One or two cycles in the idealised model, 4 cycles on a real Core i7 L1.
- **Miss penalty** $T_p$ is the *additional* time a miss costs on top of $T_h$. Fifty to two hundred cycles to main memory, and the trend is upward: DRAM latency has improved far more slowly than clock rates.

The composite metric is the average memory access time

$$\text{AMAT} = T_h + m \cdot T_p .$$

The asymmetry in that formula is the whole point: $T_h$ is paid on *every* reference, $T_p$ only on the fraction $m$. A frequent slip is to start from $(1-m)T_h + m(T_h + T_p)$ — which is correct and identical — and then "simplify" it to $(1-m)T_h + m T_p$, which is not.

This also explains a habit the course insists on: quote the **miss** rate, never the hit rate. Take $T_h = 1$ and $T_p = 100$. At 97% hits, $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.03 \cdot 100 = 4$ cycles. At 99% hits, $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.01 \cdot 100 = 2$ cycles. Two percentage points of hit rate — a 2% "improvement" by the usual reading — halve the memory time, because $\partial \text{AMAT} / \partial m = T_p$ is enormous. Hit rate compresses precisely the region where all the variation lives; miss rate stretches it out.

sections.heading: Multi-level hierarchies: local versus global miss rate
sections.body:
With more than one level of cache the model becomes a recursion rather than a sum. The miss penalty of level $k$ is not a constant — it is the average access time of level $k+1$:

$$\text{AMAT}_k = T_{h,k} + m_k \cdot \text{AMAT}_{k+1}$$

with the recursion bottoming out at $\text{AMAT}_{\text{last}+1} = T_{\text{DRAM}}$.

Here $m_k$ is the **local miss rate**: misses at level $k$ divided by the references that actually *reached* level $k$. It is distinct from the **global miss rate** $g_k = m_1 m_2 \cdots m_k$, which divides by all CPU references. Expanding the recursion gives the equivalent flat form

$$\text{AMAT} = T_{h,1} + \sum_{k \ge 1} g_k \, T_{h,k+1},$$

with $T_{h,\text{last}+1}$ read as the DRAM latency. Conflating the two rates is the single most common error on this material. An L2 with a 25–40% *local* miss rate sounds broken, but it is entirely normal: L1 has already absorbed every easy hit, so what reaches L2 is the hard residue. Only $g_2 = m_1 m_2$ says anything about the program, and it will be a fraction of a percent.

The hierarchy CENG331 works with is the Intel Core i7: per-core L1 i-cache and d-cache of 32 KB, 8-way, 4-cycle access; a per-core unified L2 of 256 KB, 8-way, 11 cycles; a shared L3 of 8 MB, 16-way, 30–40 cycles; block size 64 bytes at every level. All of it is on the CPU chip. CS:APP's Figure 6.39 gives slightly different latencies for the same machine (L2 at 10 cycles, L3 at 40–75) and quotes the penalties as roughly 10 cycles for an L1 miss served by L2, 50 for one served by L3, and 200 from main memory.

One derived fact is worth memorising because it drives the design. The L1 d-cache has $S = 32\,\text{KB} / (8 \times 64\,\text{B}) = 64$ sets, so $s = 6$ and $b = 6$: the twelve low-order bits of the address select the set and the byte. On the i7 those twelve bits are exactly the page offset, which is identical in the virtual and physical address. Set selection can therefore begin from the virtual address while the TLB is still translating — the cache lookup and the address translation overlap instead of serialising.

sections.heading: Where the misses come from: the three Cs
sections.body:
To improve a miss rate you must know which kind of miss you have, and the course's taxonomy splits them three ways.

A **cold** (compulsory) miss is the first reference to a block: the cache was empty, and no organisation could have helped. For a sequential scan of 4-byte elements the compulsory miss rate is $4/B$ — one miss per $B/4$ accesses — so cold misses answer to **block size** and to nothing else.

A **capacity** miss happens because the working set of active blocks is larger than the cache. It would occur even in a fully associative cache of the same size, so it answers to **cache size** (or, on the software side, to shrinking the working set).

A **conflict** miss happens when the cache is big enough but the mapping puts several live blocks in the same set. The slides' canonical example: with blocks restricted to position $i \bmod 4$, the reference stream $0, 8, 0, 8, \ldots$ misses every single time even though the cache is nearly empty. Conflict misses answer to **associativity**, and on the software side to padding and to changing array layouts.

The subtlety that exams exploit is that this classification is *defined relative to a baseline*. A miss is a conflict miss precisely when it would have hit in a fully associative cache of equal capacity — under an optimal replacement policy. That last clause matters. Replace the baseline's policy with LRU and the accounting can go negative: a cyclic reference pattern whose period slightly exceeds the associativity makes LRU miss on every access, so a direct-mapped cache of the same capacity can genuinely beat a fully associative LRU one. The three Cs are a diagnostic vocabulary, not a conservation law.

sections.heading: The design knobs and what each one costs
sections.body:
Every parameter in $(S, E, B)$ trades one term of the AMAT equation against another, which is why real hierarchies look the way they do.

**Cache size $C$.** A larger cache raises the hit rate, but large memories are harder to make fast, so it also raises the hit time. That single tension explains the entire hierarchy: L1 is small because it must answer in a few cycles, L3 is large because it only has to beat DRAM.

**Block size $B$.** Larger blocks exploit spatial locality and drive the compulsory miss rate down as $1/B$. But for a fixed $C$ they leave fewer lines, which hurts programs whose locality is temporal rather than spatial, and they lengthen the transfer, which raises the miss *penalty*. Modern machines settle at 64 bytes.

**Associativity $E$.** Higher associativity reduces thrashing from conflict misses. It is expensive: more tag bits per line, more replacement state, and $E$ parallel comparators. It can raise the hit time through that added complexity, and even the miss penalty, since choosing a victim takes work. The classical compromise is low associativity near the top, where the miss penalty is only a few cycles and hit time is king, and higher associativity further down — hence 8-way L1 and L2 but 16-way L3 on the i7.

**Write policy.** Write-through is simpler and lets a write buffer work independently of the cache; read misses are cheaper because they never trigger a write-back. Write-back produces far fewer transfers, which matters more the further down you go, since transfer times grow. CS:APP's advice is to reason about your *code* as if every level were write-back with write-allocate: it is the trend, and it makes writes symmetric with reads, so the same locality reasoning covers both.

Note what is *not* on this list: nothing here is under a programmer's control. The knobs a programmer actually has are the access pattern and the data layout, which is the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: From the model to the code: stride, loop order, blocking
sections.body:
The model becomes useful the moment you can predict $m$ from a loop nest, and for C arrays that prediction is mechanical. C is row-major, so `a[i][j]` sits at $\text{base} + (iN + j)\cdot \texttt{sizeof(elem)}$. Walking $j$ is stride 1: one miss per $B/\texttt{sizeof(elem)}$ accesses, a miss rate of $\texttt{sizeof(elem)}/B$. Walking $i$ walks a column with stride $N$: once $N \cdot \texttt{sizeof(elem)} \ge B$ every access lands in a fresh block and the miss rate is 1. Same data, same number of operations, a factor of $B/\texttt{sizeof(elem)}$ difference in memory traffic.

The course applies this to matrix multiply under a clean set of assumptions — 32-byte blocks holding four 64-bit words, $N$ large enough that $1/N \approx 0$, and a cache too small to hold multiple rows — and then simply reads the inner loop of each of the six loop permutations. For `ijk`, the inner loop steps `a[i][k]` with stride 1 (0.25 misses per iteration), `b[k][j]` with stride $N$ (1.0), and keeps `c[i][j]` in a register (0.0): 1.25 misses per iteration. For `kij` the inner loop holds `a[i][k]` fixed and steps both `b[k][j]` and `c[i][j]` with stride 1: 0.5. For `jki` two of the three references walk columns: 2.0. The arithmetic is identical in all six; the memory traffic differs fourfold.

Loop interchange only fixes spatial locality. Temporal locality needs **blocking**: partition the matrices into $b \times b$ tiles chosen so that the three active tiles, $3b^2 \cdot \texttt{sizeof(elem)}$ bytes, fit comfortably in the cache. Each tile is then loaded once and reused $b$ times before eviction, cutting traffic by roughly a factor of $b$ — the same total work, restructured so that the working set never exceeds $C$.

The measurement counterpart of all this is the **memory mountain**: read throughput plotted against working-set size and stride. Ridges running along the size axis mark the capacity boundaries of L1, L2 and L3 and expose temporal locality; slopes running along the stride axis expose spatial locality, falling away as the stride outruns the block size. It is the most compact single picture of a memory system, and the shape of your own code's mountain tells you which of the three Cs you are fighting.

worked_example.problem:
A Core i7-like machine, using the latencies from the CENG331 slides: $T_{h,1}=4$, $T_{h,2}=11$, $T_{h,3}=35$ cycles, and a DRAM access of 200 cycles. The *local* miss rates are $m_1 = 4\%$, $m_2 = 25\%$, $m_3 = 40\%$.

1. Compute the global miss rates and the AMAT.
2. The program issues 1.3 memory references per instruction and would run at CPI 1.0 if memory were free (the 4-cycle L1 hit is pipelined; only the miss path stalls). What is the real CPI?
3. You can either halve the L1 miss rate to 2% by restructuring loops, or halve the DRAM latency to 100 cycles by buying faster memory. Which is worth more?
worked_example.solution:
**1. Global miss rates and AMAT.** Multiply the local rates down the hierarchy:

$$g_1 = 0.04$$
$$g_2 = 0.04 \times 0.25 = 0.01$$
$$g_3 = 0.01 \times 0.40 = 0.004$$

Now unwind the recursion from the bottom:

$$\text{AMAT}_3 = 35 + 0.40 \times 200 = 115 \text{ cycles}$$
$$\text{AMAT}_2 = 11 + 0.25 \times 115 = 39.75 \text{ cycles}$$
$$\text{AMAT} = 4 + 0.04 \times 39.75 = \mathbf{5.59} \text{ cycles}$$

Check it against the flat form, which must agree:

$$4 + 0.04(11) + 0.01(35) + 0.004(200) = 5.59 \ \checkmark$$

Note how the four terms are distributed: the L1 hit costs 4 cycles, and the entire rest of the hierarchy adds only 1.59. Of that, half is DRAM, reached on just 0.4% of references.

**2. CPI.** Only the miss path stalls, so the stall cycles per instruction are the references per instruction times the L1 miss rate times what an L1 miss costs:

$$\text{stalls} = 1.3 \times 0.04 \times 39.75 = 2.067$$
$$\text{CPI} = 1.0 + 2.067 = \mathbf{3.07}$$

The machine spends more than two thirds of its cycles waiting on memory, at a 96% L1 hit rate.

**3. Which change wins?**

*Halve the L1 miss rate to 2%.* $\text{AMAT}_2$ is unchanged at 39.75, so

$$\text{stalls} = 1.3 \times 0.02 \times 39.75 = 1.034$$
$$\text{CPI} = 2.03 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{speedup} = 3.067/2.034 = \mathbf{1.51\times}$$

*Halve the DRAM latency to 100 cycles.* Rebuild the recursion:

$$\text{AMAT}_3 = 35 + 0.40 \times 100 = 75$$
$$\text{AMAT}_2 = 11 + 0.25 \times 75 = 29.75$$
$$\text{stalls} = 1.3 \times 0.04 \times 29.75 = 1.547$$
$$\text{CPI} = 2.55 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{speedup} = 3.067/2.547 = \mathbf{1.20\times}$$

The software change wins, and it is the one you can actually make. The reason is structural: DRAM is behind two levels of filtering and is reached on only $g_3 = 0.4\%$ of references, so halving its latency removes $0.004 \times 100 = 0.4$ cycles of AMAT. The L1 miss rate sits at the top of the recursion and multiplies *everything* below it. Amdahl's law applied to the memory hierarchy: optimise the term with the largest coefficient, not the largest latency.

pitfalls: **Confusing local and global miss rates.** An L2 local miss rate of 30% is normal and says nothing bad; the corresponding global rate $g_2 = m_1 m_2$ may be 1%. The recursion $\text{AMAT}_k = T_{h,k} + m_k \text{AMAT}_{k+1}$ takes *local* rates; the flat sum takes *global* ones. Mixing them inflates the answer by orders of magnitude.

**Double-counting the hit time.** $\text{AMAT} = T_h + m T_p$ already charges $T_h$ on every access, hits and misses alike, because a miss is detected by a lookup that failed. Writing $(1-m)T_h + m T_p$ drops the hit time on the miss path.

**Treating the miss penalty as a constant in a multi-level hierarchy.** There is no single number: an L1 miss costs $\text{AMAT}_2$, which itself depends on $m_2$, $m_3$ and DRAM. Quoting "the" miss penalty is only meaningful for a single-level cache.

**Assuming a bigger block is always better.** It lowers the compulsory rate as $1/B$, but at fixed capacity it leaves fewer lines — worse for temporal locality — and it lengthens the transfer, raising the miss penalty. There is an optimum, and on current hardware it is 64 bytes.

**Reading AMAT as execution time.** It is an average *latency*, and an out-of-order core overlaps misses with other work and with each other. A program with high memory-level parallelism can absorb misses that AMAT charges in full; a pointer-chasing loop, where every miss depends on the previous one, cannot. AMAT ranks designs, it does not predict wall-clock time.

**Forgetting that the three Cs are defined against a baseline.** A miss is "conflict" only relative to a fully associative cache of equal capacity under optimal replacement. Swap in LRU and the count can come out negative, because LRU thrashes on cyclic patterns that a direct-mapped cache survives.
applications: **The CS:APP cache lab**, which CENG331 assigns: part A is exactly the simulator in this card — parse an address trace, report hits, misses and evictions for a given $(S,E,B)$ — and part B asks you to cut the miss count of a matrix transpose under a fixed cache, which is blocking under another name.

**Tuned BLAS libraries** (OpenBLAS, BLIS, Intel MKL) pick GEMM tile sizes directly from this model: one tile dimension chosen so the working set fits L1, an outer tile so it fits L2. The same $O(N^3)$ arithmetic runs an order of magnitude faster than a naive triple loop purely because of $m$.

**Hardware performance counters.** `perf stat -e cycles,cache-references,cache-misses,LLC-load-misses` measures $m_1$ and $g_3$ on real runs, turning AMAT from a homework formula into a profiling tool that tells you whether a slow loop is memory-bound at all.

**Database storage engines** size their units of work to the hierarchy: column stores process vectors of a few thousand values so a batch stays resident in L2, and B-tree nodes are sized to a page so a lookup touches few cache lines per level.

**Concurrent data structures in the Linux kernel**, where hot per-CPU structures are declared `__cacheline_aligned` so two cores never share a 64-byte line. False sharing turns invisible coherence traffic into what looks like an inexplicable miss rate.
exam_focus: The 2018 CENG331 final asked for a filled-in hit/miss grid: `char matrix[5][5]` at address 0, summed **column-wise**, on a direct-mapped cache with 4 sets and 2-byte blocks, with `sum`, `row` and `col` in registers and a cold cache. You are expected to compute $\lfloor \text{addr}/B \rfloor \bmod S$ by hand for all 25 accesses — the code listing on this card reproduces the answer.

The last CENG331 quiz combined caches with virtual memory on one IA32 system: a direct-mapped 1 KB cache with 16-byte blocks, 1 KB pages, an 8-entry direct-mapped TLB and a one-level page table with 32-bit entries. It asked for the labelled structure diagram first, then TLB *and* L1 miss counts for `a[i][j] = i + j` over `int a[1024][1024]`, then a miss count for a loop hammering `a[0][0]` and `a[1][0]` whose answer turns entirely on whether the two addresses collide in the same set. Practise counting both caches from one address stream.

The AMAT drill in the lecture slides is the one to have automatic: hit time 1 cycle, miss penalty 100 cycles, 97% hits gives 4 cycles and 99% hits gives 2 cycles — "this is why miss rate is used instead of hit rate".

The slides and CS:APP disagree slightly on the same Core i7: the slides say L2 is 11 cycles and L3 is 30–40, while CS:APP Figure 6.39 says 10 and 40–75. In an exam, use the slide numbers and state the assumption; the marks are for the recursion, not the constant.

The matrix-multiply miss-rate analysis is worked in class for all six loop orders under fixed assumptions — 32-byte blocks, $N$ large, $1/N \approx 0$, cache too small for several rows. Know the method (read the inner loop, classify each reference by stride) rather than memorising 1.25 / 0.5 / 2.0, because the block size in the question will change.

self_check.question: A colleague reports that the L2 cache has a 35% miss rate and concludes it is badly designed. What is wrong with the reasoning, and what number should they have quoted?
self_check.answer:
Nothing is necessarily wrong with the cache. 35% is the **local** miss rate: misses at L2 divided by the references that reached L2, which are only the ones L1 already failed on. L1 has absorbed everything with easy locality, so what arrives at L2 is the hard residue and a high local rate is expected — 25–40% is ordinary.

The number that describes the *program's* behaviour is the **global** miss rate $g_2 = m_1 m_2$. With a typical $m_1 = 4\%$, $g_2 = 0.04 \times 0.35 = 1.4\%$: fewer than two references in a hundred get past L2 at all.

The number that describes the *cost* is neither one alone, but the contribution to AMAT. In the flat form

$$\text{AMAT} = T_{h,1} + g_1 T_{h,2} + g_2 T_{h,3} + g_3 T_{\text{DRAM}}$$

the L2 miss rate enters only through $g_2$ and $g_3$. To judge the design you need $m_2$ *and* $m_1$ *and* the latencies below — a local miss rate on its own is not evaluable.

self_check.question: Simulate the CENG331 final question by hand. `char matrix[5][5]` starts at address 0 and is summed column-wise (`col` outer, `row` inner) on a cold, direct-mapped cache with 4 sets and 2-byte blocks; only the matrix is accessed. How many hits and misses, and how do the misses split into the three Cs?
self_check.answer:
`matrix[row][col]` is at address $5\,\text{row} + \text{col}$. With $B = 2$ and $S = 4$: block $= \lfloor \text{addr}/2 \rfloor$, set $=$ block $\bmod\ 4$, tag $= \lfloor \text{block}/4 \rfloor$. The access order is addresses $0,5,10,15,20$, then $1,6,11,16,21$, and so on.

The resulting grid, indexed `[row][col]`:

| | c0 | c1 | c2 | c3 | c4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **r0** | m | h | m | h | m |
| **r1** | m | m | h | m | h |
| **r2** | m | h | m | h | m |
| **r3** | m | m | h | m | h |
| **r4** | m | h | m | h | m |

**10 hits, 15 misses, a 60% miss rate.**

Where the hits come from: the row stride is 5, an odd number, so consecutive rows in one column never share a 2-byte block — column 0 misses five times out of five. But moving from column $c$ to column $c+1$ shifts every address by exactly 1, so roughly half of those addresses are the odd partner of a byte already fetched. Those are the hits, and they are pure spatial locality inside a 2-byte block.

The three-way split: 13 distinct blocks are touched (25 bytes in 2-byte blocks), so **13 cold misses**. The remaining 2 misses are re-fetches of blocks already evicted — at addresses 4 and 14. A fully associative cache of the same 8-byte capacity under optimal replacement takes 14 misses on this stream, so exactly **1 capacity miss and 1 conflict miss**.

Worth knowing as a trap: the same fully associative cache under *LRU* takes 25 misses — it misses every single access. The block reference pattern has period 5 against 4 lines, the classic LRU thrashing case, so here the direct-mapped cache beats the fully associative one. That is why the conflict-miss definition specifies an optimal baseline.

self_check.question: You have a transistor budget to spend on one of two changes. (A) Double L1 from 32 KB to 64 KB: the L1 miss rate falls from 4% to 3%, but the hit time rises from 4 to 5 cycles. (B) Double L2 associativity from 8 to 16 ways: the L2 local miss rate falls from 25% to 20%, but the L2 hit time rises from 11 to 13 cycles. Everything else is as in the worked example ($T_{h,3}=35$, $m_3 = 40\%$, DRAM 200). Which do you choose?
self_check.answer:
Compute the AMAT for each. From the worked example, $\text{AMAT}_3 = 35 + 0.40 \times 200 = 115$ cycles in all three cases, and the baseline is $\text{AMAT} = 4 + 0.04 \times 39.75 = 5.59$ cycles.

**Option A — bigger L1.** $\text{AMAT}_2$ is untouched at 39.75.

$$\text{AMAT}_A = 5 + 0.03 \times 39.75 = 6.19 \text{ cycles}$$

That is **worse than doing nothing**. Decompose it: the extra hit cycle is paid on 100% of references ($+1.00$), while the miss-rate gain is worth $(0.04 - 0.03) \times 39.75 = +0.40$ cycles saved. Net $+0.60$.

**Option B — more associative L2.**

$$\text{AMAT}_2 = 13 + 0.20 \times 115 = 36 \text{ cycles}$$
$$\text{AMAT}_B = 4 + 0.04 \times 36 = 5.44 \text{ cycles}$$

An improvement of 0.15 cycles. Decomposed: the 2 extra L2 hit cycles are paid only on the 4% of references that miss L1 ($+0.08$), while the deeper miss-rate gain is worth $0.04 \times 0.25 \times 115 - 0.04 \times 0.20 \times 115 = 0.23$ cycles. Net $-0.15$.

**Choose B.** The principle generalises and is why L1 caches stay small and direct-mapped-ish while lower levels grow fat and associative: a change to level $k$'s *hit time* is multiplied by $g_{k-1}$, the fraction of references that reach it, but so is its miss-rate improvement. At L1 that fraction is 1, so hit time dominates every other consideration. Further down, $g_{k-1}$ is small, hit time barely registers, and you can afford whatever complexity buys a lower miss rate.

key_points: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; hit time is paid on every access, penalty only on misses.
Multi-level: the miss penalty of level k IS the AMAT of level k+1, so the model is a recursion.
Local miss rate divides by references reaching that level; global divides by all CPU references.
Core i7 (CENG331): L1 32 KB 8-way 4 cyc, L2 256 KB 8-way 11 cyc, L3 8 MB 16-way 30-40 cyc, B = 64 B.
Cold misses answer to block size, capacity misses to cache size, conflict misses to associativity.
Row-major stride 1 gives miss rate sizeof(elem)/B; walking a column gives miss rate 1.
tagline: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, applied recursively down L1→L2→L3→DRAM; tiny miss-rate moves swing memory time hugely.
tldr: Cache performance reduces to one equation, $\text{AMAT} = T_h + m \cdot T_p$, applied recursively: the miss penalty of each level is the average access time of the next. The leverage sits at the top — an L1 miss rate multiplies everything below it — which is why halving the L1 miss rate in software beats halving DRAM latency in hardware, and why a level's *hit time* matters in proportion to how many references reach it. The three Cs (cold, capacity, conflict) tell you which knob — block size, cache size, associativity — a given miss actually answers to.
